title: ‘Waste colonialism’ – the Turkish city carrying the weight of Britain’s pollution problem
text: An investigation shows Britain exporting vast quantities of waste to poor districts in Adana, leaving farmers with microplastics, toxic smoke, and debris while shifting pollution costs abroad.

title: State of the Climate: A Dimming, Overheated Planet, With Degraded Oceans
text: The annual climate overview links record ocean heat, northern forests and tundra turning into net emitters, and accelerating ice loss from Greenland into one risk picture.

title: Pennsylvania Confronts an Unfamiliar Climate Hazard: Wildfire Smoke
text: Smoke drifting south from Canadian wildfires has pushed Pennsylvania child-care providers to treat air quality as a new everyday governance problem.

title: Watching the Atlantic: Could tropical waves exiting Africa make it past the wind shear?
text: The piece tracks whether tropical waves leaving Africa can survive wind shear, offering early signals on Atlantic cyclone formation.

title: ‘The Earth itself was screaming out:’ Bay Mills Indian Community fights pipeline permitting while enveloped in wildfire smoke
text: Amid wildfire smoke, the Bay Mills Indian Community is opposing a proposed 99-year extension for a pipeline permit, with the dispute centering on permitting and sovereignty.

title: New Amazon Data Center Stokes Worry It Would Be the Most Polluting Power Plant in the U.S.
text: Amazon’s investment in a gas-fired plant for a major Texas data center raises the question of whether AI-scale infrastructure is colliding with climate pledges.

title: Extreme Heat Comes for the Red Chile Capital of Pakistan
text: Pakistan’s red-chile growers are being forced to adapt as extreme heat and rising costs undermine long-standing cultivation practices.

title: Learning Hub Research Grantee Spotlight: MUBS Climate Finance and Sustainability Centre
text:
The Makerere University Business School Climate Finance and Sustainability Centre argues that without understanding local investors’ risk preferences, mandate constraints, and entry barriers in blended finance, climate capital will remain overly dependent on external deal design rather than building a durable domestic mobilization mechanism.

Uganda’s updated NDC has made the 2030 financing gap explicit, turning the question of who funds climate action and who absorbs structural risk into an immediate policy problem. The project also seeks to translate findings into reusable lessons for Africa.

This is upstream research within the broader agenda of domestic capital participation in blended finance structures, feeding into later investment design and policy engagement.

title: Factcheck: How nuclear, gas, wind and solar power are affected during heatwaves
text:
By comparing nuclear, gas, wind, and solar performance during heatwaves, Carbon Brief shows that power-system fragility does not come only from ‘intermittent’ renewables; warmer rivers, weaker cooling capacity, and demand spikes also constrain nuclear and gas supply, so resilience must be redesigned around technology-specific climate risks.

The 2026 European heatwaves have made supply constraints in France, Romania, Hungary, and Switzerland concrete, and the piece corrects power-planning assumptions under sustained warming. It also challenges narratives that reduce system stress to wind and solar alone.

It sits at the intersection of power reliability, climate adaptation, and energy transition, with direct agenda relevance for European electricity planning and heat-risk governance.

title: Eyes on Asia: shaping the global energy transition
text:
E3G argues that Asia is becoming the निर्णative arena for the global energy transition not merely because demand is growing fast, but because cooling needs, industrial expansion, and renewable deployment are rising together, forcing states to treat power systems, industrial policy, and financial mobilization within one transition frame.

The piece responds to a narrow but decisive window in which most new global energy demand over the next decade will come from Asia, making regional policy choices globally path-defining. It also warns against treating Asia merely as an implementation arena in climate diplomacy.

This is a strategic research input for framing Asia’s energy transition narrative and policy coordinates, linking to international energy cooperation and climate finance positioning.

title: Q&A: What is in China’s new five-year plan for climate change?
text:
Carbon Brief’s overview shows that China’s new five-year climate plan is tying targets, policy tools, and implementation more tightly together, implying that central planning is not mere signaling but a way to discipline local and sectoral action through coordination and institutionalized accountability.

The plan has just been released, making this the right moment to read China’s next round of climate governance instruments and implementation logic. It also offers clues for assessing China’s policy room in the next phase of international climate talks.

It sits at the start of China’s domestic climate policy cycle and will shape the credibility of subsequent external commitments and international negotiations.

title: Leveraging “Enabling Power” Through Awarding in Global Climate Governance: Catalytic Impacts of UNFCCC’s Global Climate Action Award
source: Aron Teunissen, Sander Chan · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using the UNFCCC’s Global Climate Action Award, the authors examine how awarding mechanisms can amplify the replicability and diffusion of nonstate climate action through reputational incentives. But the extent of ‘catalytic impact’ depends on whether the mechanism addresses the key barriers actors face. The article shows that awards are not neutral recognition; they are mobilizing devices within global climate governance.

The article uses a conceptual framework and mechanism analysis centered on ‘enabling power’ to assess how awarding mechanisms shape catalytic impact.

Read it alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief signal on China’s new five-year climate plan: one piece asks how central planning disciplines implementation, the other how the UNFCCC uses awards to amplify action.

How do awards alter policy diffusion in climate governance? climate governance awards diffusion reputational incentives When do reputational incentives fail in transnational climate action? reputation transnational networks catalytic impact climate action

title: The Apocalyptic Climate Imaginary as Biopolitics: Avoid, Prepare, Endure (SI)
source: Diana Eriksson Lagerqvist, Johannes Stripple · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article treats the apocalyptic climate imaginary as a biopolitical formation, arguing that collapse is not a one-off rupture but a chronic, uneven, and increasingly normalized governing condition. It distinguishes avoidance, preparation, and endurance as three orientations, showing that futures are actively redistributed through knowledge regimes, hierarchies of worth, and subject formation.

The article draws on Foucault and Lemke to conduct conceptual analysis and discourse interpretation.

Read it alongside Inside Climate News’s Pennsylvania wildfire-smoke story: smoke is not just an event, but something that normalizes ‘preparation’ and ‘endurance’ in everyday governance.

How does disaster imagination govern adaptation? biopolitics climate imaginary adaptation governance Who is expected to endure climate collapse? inequality subject formation resilience climate governance

title: Learning Hub Research Grantee Spotlight: Genesis Analytics
text:
Climate Policy Initiative’s Learning Hub, by commissioning Genesis Analytics to study pension and insurance capital in Kenya, Nigeria, and Namibia, argues that Africa’s climate-finance bottleneck is not only a capital gap but a regulatory one: accounting rules and capital requirements keep domestic institutional investors anchored in sovereign debt rather than renewable energy, green hydrogen, water security, and resilient transport; the piece therefore points toward a blended-finance design that can work through regulatory constraints.

The piece responds to the longstanding under-supply of climate finance to Africa at a moment when domestic institutional assets are growing. It shifts the question from external scarcity to how financial regulation can redirect local asset allocation, making it timely for the current domestic-capital mobilization agenda.

This is a technical upstream issue in the climate-finance workflow, centered on domestic mobilization rather than external inflows.

title: Q&A: Does the world need ‘carbon capture and storage’ to reach net-zero?
text:
Using the UK as an example, Carbon Brief frames CCS as a central but contested tool in national net-zero pathways: it may be indispensable for hard-to-abate sectors, yet its high costs, repeated delivery slippage, and institutional ties to fossil-fuel interests make it more a transition infrastructure requiring strict boundaries and oversight than a scalable emissions fix. The implied policy lesson is that, without clearer public-investment شروط, performance constraints, and long-term storage liability rules, CCS can become a structural excuse to delay deep decarbonization.

This Q&A responds to the renewed push for CCS in net-zero plans alongside growing controversy over its costs and credibility. It reframes the issue from whether CCS is needed to who bears failure risk and long-term liability, making it immediately relevant to current technology-pathway debates.

It sits at the intersection of national net-zero strategies, industrial decarbonization toolkits, and infrastructure investment review.

title: Catalyzing Centre of Excellence for Energy Transition: a strategic enabler for Andra Pradesh to achieve its energy transition goals
text:
Climate Policy Initiative argues that Andhra Pradesh’s jointly established Center of Excellence for Energy Transition is an enabling institutional device for turning state clean-energy targets into execution capacity: beyond filling utility gaps in system planning, storage integration, and green-hydrogen coordination, it creates a durable knowledge interface among industry, regulators, and technical teams so the 2047 net-zero goal can move from declaration into grid dispatch, investment sequencing, and implementation oversight.

The article responds to the shift in India’s state-level energy transition from target-setting to execution capacity. Because Andhra Pradesh has already set ambitious goals, the timing now concerns institution-building and utility capability rather than revisiting the vision.

It sits at the interface of state-level energy policy execution, power-system reform, and national emissions commitments.

title: What Worked: Early Wins from South Africa’s First Just Energy Transition Partnership
text:
By reviewing early results from South Africa’s first Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), E3G argues that international finance, political commitment, and coordinated planning can link coal transition to jobs, energy security, and development finance only when the energy ministry, treasury, and external funders settle into a stable division of labor; the piece effectively reframes JETP from a financing package into a governance arrangement that requires institutional coordination and credibility management.

The piece appears amid criticism that JETPs have been slow and underfunded, so it seeks to show that the partnership has not failed but needs different yardsticks. It is especially relevant as transition partnerships move toward the next round of commitment review.

It sits between G20/JETP discussions, domestic energy-transition implementation in South Africa, and the credibility of international climate finance.

title: Multilateral Climate Governance
source: Franz Baumann · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
This article places nearly half a century of UNFCCC negotiations within the broader conflict between North–South development claims and governance deadlock, stressing that mitigation is now desperately urgent but still constrained by wealth distribution, development rights, and entrenched interests. Its value is not a single solution but a clear reminder that choices between climate finance, adaptation, and mitigation are political, not merely technical.

The piece is primarily normative and historical, offering a conceptual synthesis of UNFCCC negotiations rather than an empirical quantitative study.

Read alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief CCS debate: both ask how costs and responsibilities are allocated in net-zero pathways.

Who defines the costs of net zero? net zero climate finance North-South burden sharing How should finance, adaptation, and mitigation be sequenced? adaptation mitigation climate finance sequencing

title: Accountability of Networked Climate Governance: The Rise of Transnational Climate Partnerships
text:
This article examines how transnational climate partnerships reorganize governance authority across states, firms, and nonstate actors, and how such networked governance can be held accountable. The key point is that partnerships do not simply replace states; they distribute rule-setting, implementation, and monitoring across different arrangements, making transparency, monitoring, and representation central to legitimacy.

The article uses conceptual typology and comparative analysis of transnational climate partnerships to assess accountability dimensions such as transparency, monitoring, and representation.

Read alongside this issue’s E3G analysis of South Africa’s JETP, since both examine how international partnerships translate public commitments into accountable implementation.

How can partnerships be made accountable? transnational partnerships accountability monitoring climate governance How is state authority reorganized? state authority network governance public-private climate policy

title: Climate Security: Entering a new era?
text:
By co-chairing the new Climate Security Taskforce between the climate and defense ministries, the UK is linking extreme weather, supply-chain fragility, and defense planning into one governance chain; the piece implies that leaving climate risk within a single environment ministry will not produce the budgetary, diplomatic, or early-warning tools needed to act.

The piece responds directly to the UK's taskforce announcement during London Climate Action Week, moving climate security from conceptual debate into institutional design. Its timing tests whether security agencies will embed climate risk into routine procedures.

It sits at the early institutionalization stage of climate-security mainstreaming, pointing to how defense, foreign, and climate agencies will be re-divided inside government.

title: Access to finance ‘strengthens climate resilience’ among sub-Saharan women
text:
The study links financial access for women-led households to their capacity to absorb climate shocks, showing that in sub-Saharan Africa resilience is not only about physical exposure but about whether credit, savings, and buffering mechanisms reach marginalized households; it therefore points to integrating gender-inclusive finance into adaptation finance and social protection design.

The study matters now because it pulls adaptation finance back from macro pledges to household-level access, matching current debates over whether climate finance actually reaches vulnerable groups. Without better financial access, the resilience agenda may remain trapped at the project level.

It sits at the intersection of adaptation finance, gender-inclusive finance, and accountability for development outcomes.

title: The Promissory Governance of Climate Finance
text:
The author treats climate finance as a form of promissory governance in which future results are used to sustain political authority. The GCF’s adaptation results narrative is not just an evaluation device; it helps the UNFCCC claim legitimacy under conditions of uncertain impact. The central claim is that results-oriented monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) reshapes project design toward what is easiest to approve rather than what is easiest to implement, embedding knowledge politics in finance allocation.

The article combines science and technology studies (STS) with the sociology of monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) through a conceptual analysis of the GCF adaptation portfolio.

Read alongside this issue’s New York Times Climate story on data-center electricity pricing: both ask who should bear costs and how policy instruments reallocate externalities.

How does MEL reshape project design in climate finance? climate finance monitoring evaluation learning project design legitimacy How does promissory narrative redistribute authority? promissory governance adaptation finance institutional legitimacy UNFCCC

title: The Script of the Science–Policy Interface: Performative Routines in Climate Politics
source: Jeroen Oomen, Maarten A. Hajer · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article treats the science–policy interface (SPI) as a performative script: not only knowledge content but also speech styles, citation norms, and interaction routines determine how climate knowledge gains political legitimacy. Using seven established performative routines, the authors show how political action, knowledge production, and governance expectations are jointly staged and contested.

The article draws on secondary academic literature, prior interviews, document analysis, and autoethnographic observation.

Read alongside this issue’s E3G piece on climate security: both examine how institutions turn new risks into governable objects through specific scripts.

How do SPI scripts shape policy response? science-policy interface performative routines climate politics governance Who defines legitimate knowledge in climate governance? epistemic authority coproduction governmentality climate governance

text: A bear died after becoming stranded atop an electric pole in New Mexico, in a case linked to drought pushing wildlife closer to human settlements.

title: Factcheck: No, Europe’s heatwaves are not being ‘caused’ by declining air pollution
text:
Europe’s heatwaves are not being ‘caused’ by cleaner air; greenhouse-gas-driven warming remains the main driver, while falling pollution only removes part of the masking effect. The policy implication is that climate mitigation, air-quality policy, and public communication must be separated rather than blamed on net-zero transition.

This directly answers the current misreading of Europe’s heatwaves and the political move to blame mitigation policy for rising temperatures. It shifts the debate back to long-run greenhouse-gas accumulation.

It sits at the intersection of Europe’s climate narrative and net-zero politics, shaping who gets to interpret extreme weather and with what policy legitimacy.

title: State of the climate: Rapidly developing El Niño raises chance of record-warm 2026
text:
Carbon Brief treats the rapidly intensifying El Niño as a key short-term mechanism raising the odds of a record-warm 2026, but stresses that it operates on top of long-run greenhouse-gas warming. The governance implication is that climate-risk management must move beyond year-to-year variability and embed early warning, adaptation, and extreme-event preparedness into routine policy.

The analysis matches the timing of unusual warming in the first half of 2026 and concurrent European heatwaves, explaining how short-term ocean-atmosphere dynamics amplify an already elevated baseline. It also provides a temporal anchor for risk expectations into late 2026 and 2027.

It sits at the operational layer of climate services, early warning, and adaptation planning, helping governments and financial institutions refresh risk scenarios.

title: From Bonn and London to Antalya – what’s needed to build success by COP31
text:
E3G argues that if COP31 is to avoid a repeat of Bonn’s stalled negotiations, it must build a much stronger bridge between the UNFCCC process and the implementation already advancing across governments, financial institutions, and business. Otherwise, negotiations will keep producing low-density text while implementation momentum fails to translate into trust and stronger commitments.

This responds to the post-SB64 gap: limited progress in the negotiation rooms, but accelerated implementation narratives outside them during London Climate Action Week. It turns that contrast into an organizing problem for COP31.

It is embedded in COP31 preparation and the UNFCCC intersessional timeline, seeking to institutionalize implementation as part of the negotiation outcome.

title: Securing additional finance to boost the credibility of EU Clean Trade Partnerships
text:
E3G argues that EU Clean Trade Partnerships will look hollow without additional finance and therefore struggle to win partner-country trust. The remedy is to bundle trade, industrial policy, and financial support so that de-risking and clean transition become executable together.

The piece appears amid rising protectionism and volatile geopolitics, and tries to give EU clean cooperation a financing base. It moves “partnership” from diplomatic language toward funding conditions.

It sits in the construction phase of the EU’s external economic tools and clean-industry cooperation framework, with credibility as the central design problem.

title: Structural Causes and Regime Consequences: Regimes as Intervening Variables
text:
Krasner asks whether international regimes are merely by-products of power or whether they can independently structure state behavior. By defining regimes as principles, norms, rules, and decision-making procedures around specific issue areas, the article shows how institutions shape legitimacy, expectations, and the boundaries of acceptable cooperation. Its lasting contribution is to hold together two claims often treated separately: power creates rules, but rules also organize how power is exercised. This makes the article useful for reading climate negotiations, development finance, and institutional reform as contests over the force and meaning of commitments.

Read with Carbon Brief’s heatwave factcheck in this issue: the dispute is not only over facts, but over who can turn facts into an accepted governance narrative.

How do extreme-weather narratives shape regime rules? climate governance regime theory narrative politics extreme weather When do institutions strengthen commitment constraints? international institutions commitment compliance legitimacy

title: International Regimes, Transactions, and Change: Embedded Liberalism in the Postwar Economic Order
text:
Ruggie explains why the postwar economic order did not simply restore laissez-faire liberalism, but embedded open markets within domestic commitments to employment, welfare, and policy space. The concept of embedded liberalism shows that international economic rules become durable only when external openness is balanced by domestic social protection. The article matters because it treats the open order as a political settlement, not a neutral market arrangement. It is especially useful for interpreting green industrial policy, climate finance conditionality, and disputes over the development space available to poorer countries.

Read alongside E3G’s piece on EU Clean Trade Partnerships: open cooperation often depends on whether external openness is embedded in domestic development and industrial space.

Can clean trade preserve policy space? embedded liberalism trade policy industrial policy policy space How do green partnerships gain legitimacy? green industrial policy legitimacy climate finance trade partnerships

title: EU ETS Proposal: Mixed signals for investment in industrial decarbonisation
text:
The Commission’s ETS proposal weakens the expected stability of carbon pricing and complementary policy for industrial decarbonisation, raising capital costs and lengthening payback periods for firms already investing in transition. The implied argument is that co-legislators should restore investment predictability through a clearer, stronger policy mix, and anchor industrial competitiveness in stable decarbonisation rules rather than deregulation.

This commentary responds directly to the current legislative struggle over ETS revision and industrial competitiveness in the EU. It links “strategic autonomy” to policy credibility, challenging the idea that short-term concessions can buy industrial support.

The item sits in the legislative coordination phase of the EU ETS revision and industrial policy package.

title: Debriefed 17 July 2026: UK ‘firewave’ | Fossil-fuelled heat deaths | London’s Natural History Museum spotlights climate
text:
The roundup reframes the UK ‘firewave,’ fossil-fuel-driven heat deaths, and public communication as a systemic risk amplified by the energy system, urban heat exposure, and public health capacity. Its implicit claim is that policy should move beyond post hoc response and integrate mitigation, heat-health warning, and urban adaptation into one governance frame.

The roundup tracks the July European heatwave and UK extreme heat debate, showing that heat risk is shifting from “weather anomaly” to a normal governance concern. It also provides timely context for debates on health systems and urban infrastructure.

It sits in the agenda-setting phase of UK heat-health and climate adaptation policy debates.

title: Structural Causes and Regime Consequences: Regimes as Intervening Variables
text:
Krasner asks whether international regimes are merely by-products of power or whether they can independently structure state behavior. By defining regimes as principles, norms, rules, and decision-making procedures around specific issue areas, the article shows how institutions shape legitimacy, expectations, and the boundaries of acceptable cooperation. Its lasting contribution is to hold together two claims often treated separately: power creates rules, but rules also organize how power is exercised. This makes the article useful for reading climate negotiations, development finance, and institutional reform as contests over the force and meaning of commitments.

This issue’s ETS revision dispute can be read through this article: why policy signals alter the force of rules, and how co-legislators shape investor expectations through institutional design.

Ruggie explains why the postwar economic order did not simply restore laissez-faire liberalism, but embedded open markets within domestic commitments to employment, welfare, and policy space. The concept of embedded liberalism shows that international economic rules become durable only when external openness is balanced by domestic social protection. The article matters because it treats the open order as a political settlement, not a neutral market arrangement.
